subject: Speeding up Stan code for mark recapture model

messages.author: 225b847c1502aae6
messages.subject: Speeding up Stan code for mark recapture model
parts:
Hello, I'm new user to Rstan and I was trying to fit a mark recapture model using Rstan (see model 1). The problem is that the stan code is relatively slow comparing to Jags with respect to running time.  In terms of effective sample size/time stan is comparable to jags for small datasets, but falls behind as the size of the dataset grows. I have tried to vectorize the code as suggested in the user manual  (see model 2 -- note that the way I implemented this required me to transpose some of the inputted data), but the speed and ess are more or less the same.  Do you have any suggestions for speeding the code up?

Thank you so much,
Hongyuan Wang

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan code for mark recapture model
parts:
You don't need the truncation in:

sigma_z ~normal(0,5)T[0,];

because 0 and 5 are constants and sigma_z is constrained > 0.

I'd think about adding stronger priors to things like delta. Do
you really expect values in the 10,000s?

The normals can be vectorized, which should speed things up.
You'll need to break y down into two arrays, which could be challenging
given that your data looks ragged. The other thing to do is create
an intermediate array, copy the values into it, then use vectorization.
This is faster in Stan (though it would be slower in JAGS/BUGS or
in R) --- loops are fast in Stan, calls to functions over parameters
are relatively slow.

I don't really understand the model, but if you can reformulate
to use bernoulli_logit parameterization, that will be faster than
explicitly applying the inv_logit transform.

y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha)

=def=

y ~ bernoull(inv_logit(alpha))

So instead of:

p[i,j] <- inv_logit(beta[1]+beta[2].*y[i,j+1]);
...
X[n,j] ~bernoulli(p[n,j-1]);

use just:

X[n,j] ~ bernoulli_logit(beta[1] + beta[2] .* y[n,j]);

(You should double-check the indexing.)

If you really want to optimize, something like this should be two loops:

for(i in 1:N){
likechi[i]<- chi[i,l[i]];
likephi[i]<- 1;
for (k in f[i]:(l[i]-1))
{
likephi[i]<- likephi[i] .* phi[i,k];
}
}

One for the likechi, and one for the likephi. Loops are essentially
free in Stan, but the goal is to localize memory access in arrays,
which means walking over arrays separately. Bringing in data from
memory into cache is an order of magnitude slower than an arithmetic
operation or a copy operation.

- Bob

messages.author: 225b847c1502aae6
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan code for mark recapture model
parts:
Thanks Bob.  This was very helpful!!   We have implemented these changes but still see little improvement.  We have done some more investigating and found that the problem (time wise) is due to combining z_obs (observed data) and z_mis (missing data) into the array y, which we subsequently model as in your partially known parameters example in section 9.2 of the help file.  We do not know how to model z_obs and z_mis separately as in section 9.1 as y is a covariate for other data components in the model.  Can you give us any insight as to how we can speed up this section of the code in such a situation?  If we only consider the case where y is fully observed then speed in STAN is comparable to JAGS.  However, once we include the missing data structure, we have a 3-fold increase in running time in STAN vs a negligible increase in JAGS.

Thanks,
Hongyuan Wang

Andrew,

We compared time per effective sample size. But with our code even though Stan has relatively high effective sample size, its speed is about twice lower than Jags, which makes the time/neff smaller than Jags. And we figured out that the missing data coding part might be the reason.

Thanks,
Hongyuan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding up Stan code for mark recapture model
parts:
On 11/21/13, 11:23 AM, Hwa235 wrote:
> Andrew,
>
> We compared time per effective sample size. But with our code even though Stan has relatively high effective sample
> size, its speed is about twice lower than Jags, which makes the time/neff smaller than Jags.

Presumably you mean the other way around, because lower time/n_eff
is better.

> And we figured out that the
> missing data coding part might be the reason.

Can you send your most recent model and the data (or at
least some indication of data sizes)? I'd like to see if
we can recreate what you're seeing here. Having specific
models to tune can bring up issues in our code that we can
optimize.

- Bob

Yes you are right, what I mean is neff/time.

Thanks a lot!

Hongyuan
